title: 🪟 Windows: Get Ubuntu Ready
text:
🏠 Why Ubuntu?
The workshop’s tools are made for Linux. Ubuntu is a version of Linux, and WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) is the part of Windows that runs it.

🪟 Windows is your house: your browser, your files, the apps you know.
🐧 Ubuntu is a room inside it: a window where you type commands. All the workshop’s work happens in this room.
🌐 Your Windows browser still opens what you make.

You never need to leave Windows, and nothing on Windows is removed.
Why not just use PowerShell? The slides’ commands, and the way we tested the setup, are all for Linux. Ubuntu is a widely used, well-supported Linux, so what you type matches the slides and there is less to go wrong. Some tools also have Windows installers, but their paths and commands differ, and we cannot help you debug each variant on the day.

Before you start

⏱️ About 20 minutes and one restart.
🛡️ An administrator account on this computer. On a work laptop, ask IT first; if IT types the password for you, stay signed in as yourself. If you can’t get one, tell the organiser before the day.
🪟 Windows 11, or Windows 10 version 2004 or newer. To check: Settings → System → About.
🔌 Plugged in, on strong internet: Ubuntu is a big download.
📱 Open this page on your phone too, at project-delphi.github.io/quarto-workshop/windows-setup.html. The restart closes your browser.


How to use the page: do one step, compare your screen with ✅ You should see, then go on. Grey boxes hold commands, with a copy button in the top-right corner. Dashed boxes show what to expect: don’t type those. Something looks different? Go to 🆘 Stuck?.

1️⃣ Open PowerShell as administrator
PowerShell is a Windows window for typing commands. You need it for a few minutes only.

Press the Windows key (it shows the Windows logo), or click the Windows logo on the taskbar, and type PowerShell.




Drawing of the taskbar’s Start button, circled, and the search box with PowerShell typed in. It is an illustration of Windows 11: on Windows 10 the button sits at the left, and the steps are the same.



Right-click “Windows PowerShell” and choose Run as administrator.




Drawing of the right-click menu with “Run as administrator” circled.



Choose Yes when Windows asks.


✅ You should see a window whose title starts with “Administrator”. Its last line looks like this:
PS C:\WINDOWS\system32>



Drawing of the window you should see: the title says “Administrator: Windows PowerShell” and the last line ends in >.

2️⃣ Turn on WSL

Click the copy button on the box below.
Go to the PowerShell window and press Ctrl+V to paste. (Nothing? Right-click once in the window.)
Press Enter, then wait.

wsl --install -d Ubuntu --no-launch
Watch it once: this is what the window does. It repeats, and it is only a picture.

Windows PowerShell─ ▢ ✕



✅ You should see a message that you must restart, such as “Changes will not be effective until the system is rebooted”. Go to step 3.
No restart message, and it says Ubuntu is installed or “already exists”? Skip to step 5.

Save your work, then Start → Power → Restart. Come back to this page afterwards (or use your phone).

4️⃣ Download Ubuntu
The first run only prepared Windows. This run gets Ubuntu itself.

Open a normal PowerShell window, not as administrator: press the Windows key, type PowerShell, and press Enter. Ubuntu is installed for the account that runs this line, so it must be yours.
Paste the same line and press Enter:

wsl --install -d Ubuntu --no-launch
This is the long wait: the download can take many minutes. Leave the window open, even if the percentage stays still for a while.

✅ You should see that it finished, or “already exists”. Both mean go on. Keep this window open.


You are about to have two windows. Their last line tells you which is which:









🟦 PowerShell
🐧 Ubuntu




Its line ends in
> , like PS C:\Users\Ana>
$ , like ana@LAPTOP:~$


Use it for
steps 1, 2, 4 and 6 only
everything else in the workshop

section: 5️⃣ Open Ubuntu and pick a username and password
text:
5️⃣ Open Ubuntu and pick a username and password

Press the Windows key, type Ubuntu, and press Enter. A new window opens. The first start unpacks files: wait.
Username: type one short word in lower case, with no spaces, such as ana, and press Enter. It does not need to match your Windows name.
Password: type a password you will remember and press Enter, then type it again.


🙈 Nothing appears while you type the password. No dots, no stars. This is normal: keep typing and press Enter. Write the password down. You will need it again in step 8.


✅ You should see a line like this, with your own names:
ana@LAPTOP:~$
This line is called the prompt. It means “ready for a command”:



Part
Means




ana
you


LAPTOP
this computer


~
you are in your home folder


$
type here




Try it. In the Ubuntu window (the line ending in $, not PowerShell), type this and press Enter. whoami prints the name of the user you are:
whoami

ana@LAPTOP: ~─ ▢ ✕



✅ You should see your own username (not ana) on the next line, then the prompt again. Then step 5 is done:
ana

section: 6️⃣ Check that Ubuntu is on WSL version 2
text:
6️⃣ Check that Ubuntu is on WSL version 2
Click the PowerShell window (its line ends in >), paste this, and press Enter:
wsl -l -v

Windows PowerShell─ ▢ ✕



✅ You should see Ubuntu with a 2 in the VERSION column, something like this:
  NAME      STATE           VERSION
* Ubuntu    Running         2

Does it say 1? Type wsl --set-version Ubuntu 2, press Enter, and wait until it finishes.
📨 Post a screenshot of this in Discord, so the organiser knows you are ready: press Windows key+Shift+S, drag over it, then press Ctrl+V in Discord.
Now type exit and press Enter to close PowerShell. You are done with it, unless the stuck table sends you back.

text:
8️⃣ Install two small tools
Paste this into Ubuntu and press Enter:
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y curl git







Word
Means

“do this as administrator”. It asks for your Ubuntu password from step 5 (hidden again)


apt
Ubuntu’s app installer

“and then, if that worked”



A lot of text scrolls past. That is normal. Wait for the $ to come back, then check:
curl --version && git --version

title: 🪟 Windows: Get Ubuntu Ready
text:
9️⃣ Four habits for the workshop
🏠 Stay in your home folder. Keep workshop folders there, not in Documents, Desktop or OneDrive. If the prompt shows /mnt/c, you are in a Windows folder: run cd ~ to go home.
📂 See your files in Windows. This opens the current folder in File Explorer, so you can double-click what you made. The dot means “this folder”. Try it now:
explorer.exe .
➕ Open a second tab. Later you will need one, while your coding assistant is busy in the first. Press Ctrl+Shift+D. If nothing happens, your window has no tabs: open Ubuntu again from the Start menu. A second window works just as well.
🔗 Copy sign-in links whole. Ubuntu may not be able to open your browser, so tools print a link. Select all of it, copy it, and paste it into your Windows browser. A link cut in two will fail. Does the website then show a code? Copy it and right-click to paste it back into Ubuntu.

🚫 Don’t install the Windows versions of Quarto, Python or the coding assistant for this workshop. Ubuntu needs its own copies, and the Windows ones can get in the way. The next slides install everything inside Ubuntu.

Tomorrow, or after a restart: press the Windows key, type Ubuntu, and press Enter. Your files are still there.

title: Quarto Workshop
text:
Quarto = Markdown → Anything





🆓 Free and open source · no licence to buy, for anyone · MIT License
📚 All Quarto output formats · Quarto logo: Posit, PBC

Say this early: Quarto costs nothing and needs no licence key, for individuals, universities and companies alike. The Quarto CLI is under the MIT License from version 1.4 (GNU GPL v2 before that), and the tools it bundles have their own open-source licences (https://quarto.org/license.html, checked 2026-11-06). The paid part of today is the coding assistant, a separate tool: the next slides come back to that. Pandoc converts the Markdown. Code cells run in Jupyter (Python) or knitr (R), and their results are inserted. Quarto’s principal languages are Python, R, Julia and Observable JavaScript ({ojs} cells, run in the reader’s browser); Jupyter kernels add many more, such as MATLAB or Java (https://quarto.org/docs/faq/, https://quarto.org/docs/computations/ojs.html). knitr’s engines run {sql}, {c} and {bash} cells (https://pkg.yihui.org/rmarkdown-book/language-engines.html); in Jupyter, ! lines run shell commands (https://quarto.org/docs/computations/execution-options.html#shell-commands). Today we use Python only. The official list groups documents (HTML, PDF, MS Word, OpenDocument, ePub), presentations (Revealjs, PowerPoint, Beamer), Markdown flavours, wikis and more (Jupyter, JATS, RTF, …): https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/all-formats.html. ePub is the e-book format: https://quarto.org/docs/reference/formats/epub.html. Websites and blogs (https://quarto.org/docs/websites/) and dashboards (https://quarto.org/docs/dashboards/) are built from the same files. All checked 2026-10-30. The Quarto logo is a Posit, PBC trademark, used here to refer to Quarto (https://quarto.org/trademark.html).

title: Quarto Workshop
text:
🚫🤖 Quarto Is Not AI


⚙️
Traditional software
same input → same output, every time


📚
Built for publishing
quality documents, slides and websites


🤖
The assistant is separate
it writes the files · Quarto turns them into formats



🔁 No AI inside Quarto: it follows your source exactly

Participants sometimes assume Quarto is an AI tool because the workshop uses a coding assistant. It is not: Quarto is open-source publishing software (built on Pandoc, with Jupyter or knitr running code) that reads Markdown and code and writes the same outputs every time for the same inputs and data. It does not generate text, code or figures by itself and sends nothing to an AI service. The coding assistant is a separate tool that writes and edits the source files on request; Quarto then renders them. That split matters for trust: the assistant can make mistakes, so you check its files, while a render is repeatable. Code cells you add run whatever code they contain, so if a cell calls an AI service, that is your code, not Quarto. See https://quarto.org/ (not yet re-checked for this slide).

title: Quarto Workshop
text:
🔁 Reproducible: Same Source, Same Result


📄
One source
text + code + data in plain files


🧮
Numbers are computed
never typed or pasted in


▶️
One command
quarto render rebuilds everything


🕰️
Versioned with git
every change saved · uv.lock pins the tools



✏️ Change one value in the data → render → table, chart and sentence all update
🏷️ git (set up next) records which version of the files produced which result

💬 You correct one number in the data. What do you retype in the report?


Reproducible means that someone else, or you in six months, can rebuild the same results from the same files with one command, and that you can see where every number came from. It is the reason for the workshop’s structure. The report is source, not a pasted result: its figures, tables and numbers in sentences are computed by code cells and inline code from the data files, so changing an input and re-rendering updates every output without retyping (the “change an input, rebuild, and explain what updated” outcome). Reproducibility depends on versioning: git, the version control tool installed in Setup, saves a numbered snapshot (a commit) of the source, data and settings together with a message saying what changed and why. Any earlier snapshot can be restored, two versions compared, and a result tied to the exact files that made it; without versions, “the same source” is whatever happens to be on the disk today. GitHub then keeps a shared copy, and the same history backs the AI usage statement: you can show what the assistant changed and what you reviewed. The project’s pyproject.toml and uv.lock are versioned too: they pin the Python packages, so a participant’s machine and a colleague’s give the same environment. This matters most with a coding assistant: it may write code that looks right and is not, so we ask it to compute from the data and then render and check, and anyone can re-run the render to confirm. Reproducible does not mean correct: a wrong analysis reproduces perfectly, so we still check results against their sources. Good answer to the check: nothing; fix the data and re-render.

section: 📶 You Need a Stable, Fast Internet Connection
text:
📶 You Need a Stable, Fast Internet Connection
🏠 before the workshop 📖 reading


⬇️
Big downloads
Ubuntu, Quarto, the assistant, Python packages, data


☁️
The assistant is online
every reply needs the connection · it stops when the Wi-Fi drops


🏠
Do setup at home
wired or strong Wi-Fi · avoid hotels, trains, firewalled work networks



🔌 Plugged in · 📵 No VPN or proxy if you can · 🧪 Test run done at home = ready

Almost every setup step downloads something: the Ubuntu image (several hundred megabytes), Quarto, uv and the Python packages, the assistant itself, and the workshop data. The coding assistant also sends every request to a model over the internet, so a poor connection shows up as long pauses, timeouts and half-finished installs, which participants often take for their own mistakes. Ask everyone to do the setup on a reliable connection, and to bring a phone hotspot as a fallback. Company networks with a proxy or TLS inspection often block downloads: raise it before the day. In the room, check that the venue Wi-Fi copes with every participant downloading at once, and say what to do if it does not.

🆘 Error? Ask an AI Chat
🏠 before the workshop 🆘 when stuck


📋
Copy
the command you ran + the full error text


🌐
Paste into a web chat
Gemini, Claude or ChatGPT in your browser, with your system (Windows + Ubuntu, or Mac)

🔁

🔒 No passwords, keys or private data in the paste

Installs fail before the coding assistant works, and sometimes the assistant itself is what fails, so the participant needs a second route that does not depend on it: a free web chat in the browser (Gemini, Claude or ChatGPT). Good habits: paste the exact command and the whole error, say the operating system (for WSL: Windows with Ubuntu on WSL), say what step of the deck you are on, and try one suggested fix at a time. Read each command before running it: a chat can be wrong, and never run a command that deletes things or asks for administrator rights without understanding why. Remove passwords, tokens, API keys and private data first (the AI-policy slide later explains why). If two suggestions fail, post the error and what you tried in Discord. This is the same habit the workshop teaches with the assistant: you direct, check and take responsibility. The room rule remains: two minutes stuck, ask.

Exercise · ⏱️ 20 min

Every system gets ready here, so nobody skips step 1. The commands install git and curl, which the next steps assume. Windows is the big one, and participants found it the hardest at the workshop of 2026-11-05. It lives on its own page, windows-setup.qmd, because a beginner needs one action at a time and a “you should see” after each, in a page that scrolls, can be kept beside the terminal, survives the restart on a phone, and is translated by the browser. The page opens with the picture of Windows as a house and Ubuntu as a room inside it, then covers the WSL install in an administrator PowerShell, the restart, the same command again in a normal window (distributions are per user, so someone else’s administrator password must not install it), the first Ubuntu start, the wsl -l -v check, copy and paste, sudo apt install curl git, four habits, and the stuck-table. The command runs twice because on current WSL, when a restart is needed, wsl --install only enables Windows features and installs no distribution (https://github.com/microsoft/WSL/blob/3.0.3/src/windows/common/WslClient.cpp#L557-L564, checked 2026-11-06). --no-launch keeps first-time setup out of the administrator PowerShell tab, whose folder would be /mnt/c/WINDOWS/system32; the Start menu’s Ubuntu opens in ~. Without administrator rights or BIOS access WSL cannot be installed: collect such participants before the day and pair them with a neighbour (no native Windows route is supported).
On a Mac, the first git opens a dialog to install Apple’s Command Line Tools (https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Getting-Started-Installing-Git), so left alone it interrupts the assistant’s install at step 4. xcode-select --install makes that a deliberate step at home (https://docs.brew.sh/Installation, which also says Homebrew needs these tools only to build from source). Quarto’s Mac download is a standalone .pkg (https://quarto.org/docs/download/). All checked 2026-11-06. Apple’s own page could not be read by the check, and the dialog’s wording and download time are not documented here. “Already installed” from that command is fine: go on. sudo asks for the Linux password, which stays hidden as you type. On other Linux, install curl and git with its package manager. Written from documentation and not yet tried on a clean Mac or a Windows machine: run both once before teaching.

Everyone, on every system: the rest of the workshop happens in a terminal, a window where you type commands instead of clicking. The picture is Ubuntu on Windows (WSL) in Windows Terminal, where Windows 11 opens 🪟 Start → Ubuntu; Windows 10’s plainer window, a Mac or a Linux terminal look different but answer the same. The terminal opens in your home folder, written ~ (here /home/ana; on a Mac /Users/ana). pwd prints the current folder, date the day and time (-05 is the time zone, as in Colombia), ls lists the folder (Ubuntu shows folders in blue), mkdir name creates a folder, cd name enters it, cd .. goes up one level and cd ~ (or cd alone) goes straight home from anywhere. 🔁 Many harnesses can run several models: same tool, different results

The model is the language model (for example Claude, GPT or Gemini). The harness is the program around it: it gives the model tools to read and write files, run commands and search, asks you to approve actions, and feeds results back in a loop. The assistants on the install slide (Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity) are harnesses; many can run several models, so the same harness behaves differently with a different model, and the same model behaves differently in a different harness. That is why the next slide is about choosing a model, and why no model is always right: check its work (the “you direct and check” rule).

Each company offers a family, from small and cheap to large and capable, and they do not all do the same job: the table is about use cases, not a ranking. Larger, more recent models usually follow longer instructions, plan multi-step work and recover from errors better, while small models are quicker and cheaper and are often enough for short, well-specified edits such as fixing a typo or reformatting a table. Hard tasks here, such as joining datasets or debugging a failed render, reward the stronger model. Good answer to the check: a small model for the typo, the strongest available for the join. If a prompt keeps failing, try a stronger model inside your assistant (see its documentation for how). For this workshop the prompts are short and well specified, so Haiku or Sonnet with the effort (reasoning) setting on medium, or ChatGPT’s Sol on low, is sufficient. Both vendors give a stronger starting point for unknown, hard work: Anthropic says to start with Opus 5.5 for most workloads, and OpenAI with GPT-6 Astra for complex reasoning and coding. Our advice is smaller because these prompts are small and it saves your credits.
Each column is in price order, and a row is not a pairing: there are no benchmarks here, Sol and Sonnet cost the same, and Terra costs half as much inside the same $$$ band. The $ tiers are fixed bands of the API list price per million input tokens, each about 3.2× (√10) the last, so two $ are 10×: $ under $0.32, $$ $0.32 to $1, $$$ $1 to $3.20, $$$$ $3.20 to $10, and $$$$$ $10 and above. Output prices are five times input for all eight models, so the bands hold for output too. List prices checked 2026-11-06 (input / output): Haiku and Luna $0.10 / $0.50, Terra $1 / $5, Sonnet and Sol $2 / $10, Opus $4 / $20, Fable and Astra $10 / $50. The slide shows bands, not dollars, because the numbers change often; a new price moves only its own model’s band. Subscriptions count usage differently. Haiku’s $ is for prompts up to 100,000 tokens; above that it costs five times as much ($$), which a long session can reach. Which models you can pick depends on your plan and tool version (Terra needs Codex CLI 0.159.0 or later). Sources, all checked 2026-11-06: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/overview, https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing, https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config, https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models, https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/models. Names and prices change often: re-check this table before each run. Gemini, used through Antigravity, is not in the table: add it if your group uses it.
📉 The 100–1000× within a few years is our expectation from the trend, not a promise: at a16z’s 10× a year, 100× takes about two years and 1,000× about three. The price of a fixed level of capability has fallen fast: for models matching a given benchmark score, a16z measured about 10× cheaper each year, 1,000× in the three years from November 2021 (LLMflation, Guido Appenzeller, 2024-11-12), and Epoch AI found 9× to 900× a year depending on the benchmark (LLM inference price trends, 2025-03-12); both checked 2026-11-07. Both track the cheapest model that reaches a score, not one model’s price list, and both say the pace may slow. Neither measures frontier work, so the price of what Fable or Astra do today may fall more slowly. The practical point: pick by task, not by today’s price.

Slash commands are typed at the assistant’s prompt, not in the shell, and they differ a little between assistants: /model opens a picker for the model and, where the assistant offers it, the effort (reasoning) level. Higher effort thinks longer: slower and dearer, but better on multi-step work; medium is enough here. Cost follows tokens, and three things raise them: a bigger model costs more per token, a higher effort writes more thinking tokens per reply, and a longer conversation is sent back to the model with every new message, so each later reply costs more than the first (prompt caching makes repeated context cheaper, not free, and the cache expires). So the habit is: small model, medium effort, one task per conversation, /clear as soon as a task is done. Plans with usage limits or API credits drain faster with long chats, big models and high effort; many assistants show usage with a command or status line (type / to look). These cost mechanics are written from general knowledge, not yet checked against each provider’s pricing pages or dated: verify before teaching. /clear drops the conversation so old instructions and files read earlier stop steering the assistant and stop using up its context window; nothing on disk changes, and the project’s AGENTS.md is read again. Starting it again in the folder begins a new session, and the files persist. Good answer to the check: /clear, because the new task needs none of the old chat. When a coding assistant starts it treats the current folder as its root, the default world it works in: it reads and edits the files there and in the folders below, and runs commands from there. The first time you start one in a folder it asks whether you trust that folder (the wording differs between Claude Code, Codex and Antigravity). Trusting it means you allow the assistant to read the files and, with your approvals, change them and run commands there, so trust only folders you created for the work, never a folder with other people’s projects, private documents or keys such as ~, ~/.ssh or Documents. Project instructions in the folder, such as AGENTS.md, are also read and followed, which is another reason to trust only your own folders. Starting inside the project folder means paths in prompts are short (data/london.csv), the project’s AGENTS.md is found, and a mistake stays inside one folder you can restore. It is not a guaranteed boundary: approve each command by reading it, because a command can still name a path outside the root. To work in another folder, leave with /exit, cd there and start again. Never run two assistants writing to one folder. The setup steps use ~/setup for the install prompt and each part uses its own project folder. section: 📜 Using AI in Research: Say It, Own It
text:
📜 Using AI in Research: Say It, Own It
🏠 before the workshop 📖 reading


🚫
Never an author
AI cannot be accountable


🔍
You verify everything
code, numbers, references


🔒
Keep private data out
unpublished or sensitive work stays out of public tools


📝
Disclose the use
tool + version · task · your checks



⚖️ Never generate or alter primary data or images: that is misconduct

💬 Which needs a statement: fixing a typo, or computing a table? · 📝 An example


Publishers’ policies differ, so read the one for your journal, course or employer before submitting. The common core, from the summary supplied for this deck (not yet checked against each publisher’s own policy page: do that before teaching, and record the date): AI tools are not listed as authors because they cannot take responsibility; the authors verify AI output, including facts and references, and answer for plagiarism; unpublished manuscripts, review reports, participant data and proprietary work are not uploaded to public AI tools. Where to disclose depends on the use. Basic copyediting (grammar, spelling) is usually exempt. Drafting or translating text goes in the acknowledgements or a declaration, with the tool and version. Data analysis and coding go in the Methods, with enough detail to reproduce them. Explanatory diagrams are disclosed in the caption or declaration. Generating or altering primary research images or raw data is prohibited. Other common forms, from the same summary: for translation, name the tool and say you reviewed the translated sections so the meaning was preserved; for a diagram made with a generative tool, say which figure, which tool and version, that you edited and labelled it, and that it fabricates no primary data; and, optionally, a statement that no AI tools were used. Publishers also differ in form: some ask for a separate AI declaration with the submission, some for a note in the cover letter, and some ban AI-generated images outright. This workshop is a reason to practise: you direct an assistant, so you will have something to disclose. The 📝 link opens this deck’s own statement, its second slide: adapt it by naming your own assistant and model exactly as your assistant names them, with the version, saying which tasks it performed, and keeping the last sentence. Good answer to the check: a typo fix is basic copyediting and is usually exempt; computing a table is analysis and belongs in the Methods, with enough detail to reproduce it, which here is the code and the AGENTS.md that the project keeps.

A free web chat such as Gemini, ChatGPT or Claude is a good place to turn a rough idea into a prompt for the coding assistant. text:
🧰 Environments: Then and Now


💻
OS
macOS · Windows · Linux


🔩
Chip
Intel/AMD x86_64 · Apple/ARM arm64


🗣️
Language
Python · R · JS … which version?


📦
Dependencies
packages · versions · compiled C




🕰️
Then
conda · compilers · PATH · kernels → ⏳ hours


⚡
Now 🐍 uv
🔒 one lockfile, every OS and chip → ⏱️ seconds



🤖 either way: the assistant sets it up · you approve


Code runs on an operating system and a chip, in some version of its language, with packages at particular versions. That holds for most languages, not just Python. Many scientific packages contain compiled C, C++ or Fortran, built separately for each OS and chip: Python ships them as wheels whose platform tag names both, such as macosx_11_0_arm64 (“compatibility with macOS 11 or later”) or manylinux_…_x86_64 (https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/platform-compatibility-tags/). Setting this up used to be a lesson of its own: install conda or a system Python, sometimes a compiler, fix PATH, register a Jupyter kernel, then debug it on each laptop. For Python, uv now does it in one step. It fetches Python too (“uv automatically installs missing Python versions as needed”, https://docs.astral.sh/uv/guides/install-python/), and uv.lock “captures the packages that would be installed across all possible Python markers such as operating system, architecture, and Python version” (https://docs.astral.sh/uv/concepts/projects/layout/), so one lockfile serves every Mac, Windows and Linux laptop in the room. Other languages pair a project file with a lockfile the same way: R’s renv.lock (https://rstudio.github.io/renv/articles/renv.html), npm’s package-lock.json (https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/configuring-npm/package-lock-json) and Rust’s Cargo.lock (https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/cargo-toml-vs-cargo-lock.html); all checked 2026-10-31. Either way, nobody needs to remember the commands: say what the project needs, and the assistant runs them while you approve. The next slide does exactly that. 🤖 Sub-Agents: One Lead, Many Hands


🧑‍✈️
Lead
your assistant: splits the work, waits, renders, checks


🤖🤖🤖
Sub-agents
one task each, own context, all at once


📄
One file each
no two agents edit or render the same file



⏱️ three tasks ≈ the slowest one · 🪙 more tokens

Claude Code · Codex · Antigravity · checked 2026-10-31

A sub-agent is a separate assistant session that the lead starts for one task: it has its own context window, does the task and reports back, while the lead waits for all of them and checks the results. Independent tasks then take about as long as the slowest one, but each sub-agent does its own model and tool work, so a run uses more tokens. Claude Code runs sub-agents in parallel when a prompt asks for them, without any set-up; its own example is “Research the authentication, database, and API modules in parallel using separate subagents” (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents). Codex enables sub-agents by default and starts them when asked; its docs warn that parallel edits “can create conflicts” and that sub-agent runs use more tokens (https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/agent-configuration/subagents). Antigravity’s CLI lets its primary agent delegate to parallel subagents (https://antigravity.google/docs/subagents?tab=cli); the docs do not say a prompt can require it, so agy may do the tasks itself. All checked 2026-10-31. Two rules keep parallel work safe, and the prompt states both: each sub-agent writes only its own files and renders nothing, and the lead renders the files one at a time, because two Quarto renders, or two uv run environment updates, in one folder can collide. Sub-agents read AGENTS.md too, so the project’s rules (cited numbers, open photos, uv run) still apply. This is the same split as this repository’s own role contracts in its AGENTS.md.

🌳 Git: Every Change, Safely

a snapshot + why

propose the change


👀
review

✅

into main



👤 today: straight to main · 👥 a team: the whole loop


Concepts, not commands: the assistant runs git and you approve. The six terms stay in English when the deck is translated, as they do in git and on GitHub. A repository is the project folder plus its full history. A commit is a snapshot of every tracked file with a message saying why, so any earlier version can be restored or compared. A branch is a movable label on a line of commits: work happens on a branch while main stays working (https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Branching-Branches-in-a-Nutshell). Push copies commits to the remote repository on GitHub. A pull request proposes merging a branch, shows the diff and collects discussion and checks (https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/collaborating-with-pull-requests/proposing-changes-to-your-work-with-pull-requests/about-pull-requests); a review comments on it, approves it or asks for changes (https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/collaborating-with-pull-requests/reviewing-changes-in-pull-requests/about-pull-request-reviews); merging adds its commits to main. All checked 2026-10-31. Working alone today, the next slides commit straight to main and push; in a team, every change goes round the loop, and this workshop’s own repository is built that way. Ask the assistant to “commit with a message that says why”, and read its diffs before you approve.

Optional, about thirty seconds, and nobody signs up for anything today: skip it if the publish block is running late. A rendered Quarto site is static files (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images), so Quarto’s docs say any web server or web host can be used: publishing is copying the output folder (_site/ for a website) to the host (Other Services). Each host here has a free plan for static sites; all were checked 2026-11-07 on the linked official pages.
There are two routes. 📤 You render on your computer and upload _site/: quarto publish does this for GitHub Pages and Netlify, and Wrangler for Cloudflare. ⚙️ The host builds the site from your Git repository: Render, a GitLab CI job, and the Git integrations of Cloudflare and Vercel. The London repository leaves _site/ out, so connecting it to a host that builds gives no site unless that build installs Quarto, Python and the project’s packages (or you commit the rendered output).

Netlify: a built-in Quarto target, uv run quarto publish netlify (Quarto docs). Quarto’s page says its Netlify build plugin renders Markdown only and runs no Python, so render locally and publish the result. The Free plan has 300 credits a month, and each production deploy costs 15 (pricing).
Cloudflare: its Pages docs now tell new projects to start with Workers, where requests for static assets are free (migration guide). wrangler deploy uploads the assets directory named in the Wrangler configuration file, so set that to _site (static assets). Pages’ Free plan allows 500 builds a month and 20,000 files (limits).
Vercel: the Hobby plan is free for non-commercial, personal use only, with 100 GB of data transfer a month (Hobby plan).
GitLab Pages: on GitLab.com’s Free tier. A .gitlab-ci.yml job publishes the public folder by default, to namespace.gitlab.io/project, so set Quarto’s output-dir: public (or change the job’s publish path) and install Quarto and Python in the job, which uses the Free tier’s CI minutes (GitLab Pages).
Render: static sites are free to deploy, count against the workspace’s monthly bandwidth and pipeline minutes, get an onrender.com URL, and rebuild on every push to the connected branch (static sites).

Quarto Pub, Quarto’s own free host, is being replaced by Posit Connect Cloud (Quarto Pub docs). We use GitHub Pages today because the repository is already on GitHub and quarto publish gh-pages is built in. Free plans change: read the current limits before choosing one (publishing guide).

A white paper is the academic version of the guide: abstract, introduction, methods, results, conclusions and references, with every number computed from data/ (the project’s AGENTS.md says so, so the prompt need not). It looks like a LaTeX article without a LaTeX install: Quarto 1.10.20 bundles Typst 0.15, which embeds New Computer Modern, the OpenType version of LaTeX’s Computer Modern (checked 2026-11-01 in the PDF’s embedded fonts). The paper’s header needs Quarto ≥ 1.10 (quarto --version): 1.6.40 stops with “unexpected argument: spacing”. section-numbering numbers the headings, bibliography reads the BibTeX file, and bibliographystyle: ieee picks Typst’s numbered style. Typst prints its own “Bibliography” heading, so the prompt asks for #set bibliography(title: [References]), which goes in the Typst format’s include-in-header; the paper then needs no References heading of its own. The finished example also wraps Quarto’s Typst article function so that the title is set in New Computer Modern too. [@key] cites a reference; @fig-…, @tbl-…, @eq-… and @sec-… refer to labelled figures, tables, equations and sections. An inline expression in a YAML abstract runs before the setup cell and fails, so the finished example writes its abstract in the body, wrapped in a raw {=typst} block. It also floats figures, draws booktabs-style table rules and sizes table columns to their contents (tbl-colwidths: false). ALVA counts only its members, so the paper says “ALVA member attractions” and treats the five sights as a description, not a sample. Genuine LaTeX output is format: pdf, which needs a TeX distribution (quarto install tinytex): https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/pdf-basics.html. Docs: https://quarto.org/docs/output-formats/typst.html, https://quarto.org/docs/reference/formats/typst.html, https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/citations.html and https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/cross-references.html (checked 2026-11-01). All sources are public Colombian open data, joined on the DANE DIVIPOLA municipality code (see examples/water/data/README.md for every table, licence and cut-off date). INS (Instituto Nacional de Salud) publishes the IRCA surveillance results (datos.gov.co nxt2-39c3); DANE supplies the list of municipalities, population projections and boundaries (and the population behind per-person spending); the IRCA table is the utility-supplied (“prestadores”) IRCA, not INS’s national total; ICFES supplies the Saber 11 exam and MEN the school dropout rate. DNP, CHIRPS and SRTM add poverty, spending, rainfall and altitude. Why it is useful: drinking-water quality is a public-health issue, but national averages hide where the risk is. Municipal data lets us see which places and which zones (urban or rural) are worst, and compare them with outcomes such as infant mortality and exam scores. Because the data and the analysis are open, anyone can check and rebuild the results, which is the point of this workshop.

🧪 tap-water samples against health limits
⚖️ failed tests weighted by risk: E. coli 25 · turbidity 15 · pH 1.5
📏 0 = no risk → 100 = unfit



🎓 Saber 11 · ICFES exam

🧑‍🎓 students finishing secondary school
📚 5 tests: reading, maths, social studies, science, English
📏 global score 0–500




🧮 both are averages: IRCA over water samples · Saber 11 over students

Resolución 2115 de 2007, arts. 13–14 (normas.cra.gov.co) · ICFES, Saber 11.° Guía de orientación 2017-1, pp. 101 and 104 (icfes.gov.co)

IRCA (Índice de Riesgo de la Calidad del Agua para consumo humano), Resolución 2115 de 2007: each tested characteristic carries a risk score (art. 13, Cuadro 6: Escherichia coli 25, total coliforms 15, turbidity 15, free residual chlorine 15, apparent colour 6, pH 1.5, among others). A sample’s IRCA is the score of the characteristics that fail their limit as a percentage of the score of all characteristics analysed, and the monthly IRCA is the mean over the month’s samples (art. 14). So 0 means every test passed and 100 means every test failed. Our irca is the year’s utility-supplied (“prestadores”) IRCA from the INS open table; the next slide shows why that matters. Saber 11 is ICFES’s standardized exam for students finishing upper secondary school, with five tests (critical reading, mathematics, social studies and citizenship, natural sciences, English). The global score is 5 × the weighted mean of the five test scores (each 0–100; English weight 1, the others 3), on 0–500 without decimals, and its mean was fixed at 250 in the first sitting (2014-2) so that years compare (guide, p. 104). Our saber11_mean is the mean global score of the students whose school is in that municipality and zone, both sittings of a year pooled; it covers only students who sat the exam, so it says nothing about those who left school. Sources checked 2026-10-30.

🧩 k-Means in Four Steps

● point◉ centre━ its path🎯 points close to their centre🧭 many rows → a few kinds to compare⏸ fix123456789101112🎲 1🎲 2🎲 3🧩 This 3-D view needs WebGL; the four steps are written in the notes. 🎯 points close to their centre · 🧭 many rows → a few kinds to compare

🎬 Short · ¿Qué es k-means?


💧 water data: k = 4 is a hyperparameter, picked from k = 2–8 by an elbow rule · silhouette stays low (about 0.2), so k is a judgement call


Synthetic toy points, labelled as such: 560 random points in 3-D around three centres, drawn by this deck with a fixed seed. The four steps: ① drop k centres at random points; ② assign every point to its nearest centre; ③ move each centre to the mean of its points; ④ repeat ② and ③ until nothing changes. → steps through the algorithm; the numbered buttons jump to a step, ▶ play runs it, 🎲 1–3 pick one of three random starts (two reach the lowest inertia, the third gets stuck: a bad start can give a worse answer, hence n_init=20), and dragging turns the cloud. The thin lines are the distances that inertia adds up. Each centre leaves a trail, thicker towards its latest position, so you can see where it started and how far it travelled; the readout gives the farthest move of each ③. Moves usually shrink, but one can grow for a step before they settle: what never rises is inertia. The centres glide slowly on purpose: this movement is the algorithm. A jump to another step or start lands at once, because a glide there would not be a path the algorithm took.
Why cluster? (1) A table of thousands of rows becomes a few kinds a person can read and name. (2) You can compare and target by kind: which places need which help. (3) It needs no labels, so it is a first look at data nobody has categorised. (4) Odd groups point to data errors or special cases. Clusters describe; they do not explain or prove causes.
🎬 The Short “But What is K-Means?” (Graduate ML, https://youtube.com/shorts/H1kB2FAjePw) opens in a player that sets 0.9× speed (checked: the player reports 0.9) and requests Spanish captions and interface. YouTube’s embed has no setting, documented or otherwise, for the audio language, so choose Spanish audio in the player’s ⚙ menu (Audio track) if the video offers it; an unavailable track is not an error here (checked 2026-11-03: none was exposed).
k-means needs k up front. It starts from k centres, assigns each point to the nearest, moves each centre to the mean of its points, and repeats until nothing changes. Different starts can end in different solutions, so we run 20 starts (n_init=20) and keep the best, with a fixed random_state for reproducibility. Inertia is the sum of squared distances from points to their centre.
Choosing k for the water data (choose_k() in analysis.py, fitted on all kept rows): k = 2 is excluded because it mostly splits urban from rural rows (adjusted Rand index with the zone 0.50). Elbow: take the smallest k ≥ 3 after which one more cluster cuts inertia by less than 10%, if its silhouette is within 0.01 of the best k ≥ 3. Here the next cluster cuts inertia by only 7% and the silhouette (−1 to 1, on a fixed sample of 5,000 rows) is 0.195. A silhouette near 0.2 is weak: the kinds overlap and summarise a continuum, which is normal for social data. Stability: refits with 5 other seeds give the same clusters (adjusted Rand index ≥ 0.998; 1 means perfect agreement). The elbow and silhouette plots are on clusters.qmd.

📉 Worse Water, More Infant Deaths?








Figure 8: Median infant mortality by utility-supplied (prestadores) IRCA band, per cluster. Infant mortality changes method in 2017, and 2020 looks like another source: 2017–2019 and 2021–2023 are pooled. Bands under 20 municipality-years are not drawn.






⚠️ descriptive only: not a causal effect of water safety


Spearman’s ρ within each cluster is between -0.04 and +0.10 (computed by irca_vs_infant(); n = municipality-years with both values, a municipality whose two zones share a cluster counted once with their mean IRCA). A flat line does not show that water is harmless either: the outcome is municipal while IRCA is zonal, blank rates (which may mean zero deaths) are left out, small municipalities have noisy rates, and confounders push in both directions. The binned medians follow the Resolución 2115 bands.

title: Quarto Workshop
text:
🤔 What Else Could Explain It?


💸
poverty


🌾
rurality


🏥
health-service access


📝
reporting quality


🔍
ecological level: municipal outcome, zone IRCA



Confounders affect both water safety and health: poorer and more rural places have worse water and worse access to clinics, and they also register fewer births and deaths. The ecological fallacy: a pattern across places need not hold for the people in them. Clusters hold some of this constant, but not all: within a cluster, places still differ in poverty and access. A causal claim would need a design that handles these, such as before/after changes in treatment plants with comparison places.

text:
Define Success Before Looking for a Winner
Primary outcome: mean two-week sales per assigned customer, in dollars.
Secondary outcomes: purchase conversion and website visit rates.
For campaign \(a\) and no-email control \(0\):
\[\widehat{\Delta}_a = \overline{Y}_a - \overline{Y}_0\]
\(Y_i\) is customer \(i\)’s two-week spending, including zero purchases. Positive \(\widehat{\Delta}_a\) estimates additional sales per assigned customer.
Check: the denominator includes every customer assigned to that arm.

Analyze assignment as an intention-to-treat comparison. Independent arm means, not paired customer differences. Random assignment supports a causal comparison for this experiment, assuming valid implementation and no interference. There is no basis for conditioning on email opens, visitors, or purchasers.

What Does Uncertainty Mean Here?
⭐ self-paced

Explain the assumptions behind the intervals. For independent arms, use customer-level sampling and preserve assignment groups. Compare men's and women's emails directly before declaring a winner. State how multiple comparisons and skewed spending affect interpretation.

Check: most customers spend zero; a few spend much more. Intervals describe estimation uncertainty under stated assumptions.

Do not use paired resampling: each customer receives one assignment. A bootstrap can sample customer rows separately within each arm and recompute each contrast; state the seed, repetitions, independence assumption, and interval method. A normal approximation needs a justification for highly skewed spending. If using many subgroup comparisons, label them exploratory and plan validation. Neither an interval nor randomization establishes applicability to a new retailer.
